newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angola's UNITA says Savimbi won't meet Christopher.
newsitem.headline: Angola's UNITA says Savimbi won't meet Christopher.

text.p: Angola's former rebel UNITA movement said on Saturday its leader would not meet U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher for talks on the southern African country's troubled peace process.
Spokesman Isias Samukuva said UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi would not travel to Luanda to meet Christopher, who stops in Angola on Monday as part of a five-nation African tour.
"I want to make it clear that Dr Savimbi will not come to Luanda to meet Warren Christopher. Political conditions are not favourable to allow this to happen," Samukuva told Reuters.
Christopher is scheduled to meet President Jose Eduardo dos Santos for discussions on the fitful two-year-old peace process which ended nearly two decades of civil war.
Savimbi has several times refused to go to the government- held capital from his stronghold in Bailundo in the north of the country, which is still effectively divided between the former foes.
He snubbed his southern African neighbours earlier this month at a summit they organized to break the deadlock.

Meanwhile UNITA sent four generals to the capital on Friday to be integrated into the country's post-war army, a positive step for the country's troubled peace process, U.N. spokesman David Wimhurst said.
The four generals included UNITA's chief of operations, General Amos Chilingutila.
U.N. special representative in Angola Khaled Yassir met the generals in Luanda after heavy rain delayed their flight from UNITA's Andulo stronghold, about 225 km (140 miles) east of the capital.
The former rebels are under threat of sanctions from the U.N. Security Council over their refusal to stick to agreements struck nearly two years ago.

The peace plan in the oil- and diamond-rich country is way behind schedule, partially because of UNITA's failure to integrate members into a restructured national army. The first five generals arrived in Luanda only last month to be integrated into the national force.

The U.N. Security Council said on Friday it would slap sanctions on UNITA if no progress is made by November 20 -- the second anniversary of the Lusaka accord which ended the war raging after independence from Portugal in 1975.

Steps could include freezing bank accounts abroad and the prevention of travel by UNITA officials. The council threatened sanctions on the movement in September 1993 but never instituted them and has since imposed an oil and arms embargo which it has had trouble enforcing.

The council extended the U.N.'s 7,200-strong peacekeeping mission in the country for just two more months, to keep the pressure on both parties. It is expected to be renewed until at least February 8, the target date for ending the operation altogether.

During the Cold War, UNITA forces were bolstered by those from South Africa's apartheid government with the acquiescence of the United States while its opponents were helped by Cuban troops backed by the then-Soviet Union.
